Every true soap is made by reacting **fats or oils** with a strong alkali. For bars, the alkali is **sodium hydroxide**, sold in Nigerian markets as caustic soda. The reaction is called **saponification**. It turns oil and caustic soda into two things: **soap** and **glycerin**. When the amounts are right, no free caustic soda is left in the finished bar.
A single bar of soap
The same reaction makes a hard laundry bar and a gentle bath bar; the choice of oils and superfat makes the difference.
How a soap molecule cleans

A soap molecule has two ends. One end loves water. The other end loves oil and grease. When you rub soap into a stained cloth, the oil-loving ends grab the grease, and the water-loving ends face outward. Many molecules gather round each droplet of grease to form a tiny ball called a **micelle**. Rinsing water then carries these balls away, with the dirt trapped inside.
Sodium soaps, made with caustic soda, are firm. Potassium soaps, made with caustic potash, are soft or liquid. That is why everything in this course uses caustic soda: we are making bars.

Two products, two design goals

A **laundry bar** works on fabric, not skin. You want it to cut grease and sweat strongly, stay hard in a wet bucket, and not leave oil on clothes. So laundry bars use a high share of PKO or coconut oil and very little spare oil. A **bath bar** touches skin every day. You want it to clean gently and leave skin comfortable, so it balances cleansing oils with conditioning oils and keeps more spare, unreacted oil in the bar.

That spare oil is called the **superfat**. A superfat of 5% means you use 5% less caustic soda than the oils could take, so about 5% of the oil stays as oil. Soap Queen, a long-running soap makers' resource, recommends about 5% for ordinary bath bars and no more than 3% for laundry soap, because extra oil can stain clothes and go rancid.

Soap and hard water

In hard water, which carries dissolved calcium and magnesium, part of the soap reacts with these minerals to form **soap scum**, the grey film you see on buckets. The scum wastes soap and can leave clothes dull. Borehole water in many parts of Nigeria can be hard. Two practical answers: use rain water or softer water for washing where possible, or add **washing soda** (sodium carbonate) to the wash water, which you will use in Module 2 to make laundry powder.
Worked example: deciding what each product needs
For example, Ngozi in Onitsha already sells palm oil. Customers ask her for a cheap bar for washing clothes and a nice bar for the bath. She plans one formula for each.
For the laundry bar she writes: main oil PKO for cleansing, some palm oil for hardness and slower wear, superfat 2% so clothes are not left oily.
For the bath bar she writes: palm oil for a hard creamy bar, PKO limited to about a fifth of the oils so it is not drying, olive and shea for conditioning, castor oil for lather, superfat 5%.
She notes that the laundry bar needs no fragrance, which saves money, while the bath bar will carry a light scent.
She tests the water in her shop's borehole by washing a white cloth with a sample bar. A grey film forms in the bowl, so she plans to sell washing soda powder beside the bars.
Ngozi has two clear design briefs before she buys a single kilogram of oil, which stops her from making one bar that does neither job well.

A woman carrying shopping bags
Buy raw materials with a checklist in hand, not on trust alone.
Oils
**Palm kernel oil (PKO):** the backbone of Nigerian laundry bars. It should be clear to light yellow when warm and smell clean and nutty. A sharp or sour smell means it is going rancid.
**Palm oil:** gives hardness and slow wear. Red palm oil colours soap orange; this is fine for laundry bars. Bleached palm oil gives a paler bar for bath soap.
**Coconut oil:** similar cleansing to PKO, usually costs more in most Nigerian markets; use whichever is better value near you.
**Shea butter:** a conditioning, hardening butter for bath bars. Unrefined shea should smell nutty and smoky, not sour.
**Olive and castor oil:** used in smaller amounts in bath bars. Check the bottle is sealed and in date.
Never use oil that has been used for frying. Food particles and breakdown products make soap smell bad and spoil faster. Avoid oils sold in unlabelled, reused containers that once held chemicals.
Caustic soda

Caustic soda is sold as **flakes, pearls or solid lumps** in sealed bags or tubs. Buy from a chemical seller who keeps it sealed and dry. It absorbs water and carbon dioxide from the air, especially in humid weather, and slowly loses strength. Signs of a bad bag: wet, sticky or clumped flakes, or a crusty white coating.

Many bags print the **purity** (assay), for example 98% or 99%. Soap calculators assume 100% pure sodium hydroxide. If your bag says 98%, divide the calculated amount by 0.98 to get the flakes you actually weigh. If there is no purity on the bag, you cannot be sure of the strength, so test a small batch first and check the bars carefully.
Worked example: correcting for caustic soda purity
For example, Amina in Kano calculates that her laundry run needs 1,625 g of pure sodium hydroxide. Her 25 kg bag is labelled 98% purity.
She divides the pure amount by the purity: 1,625 / 0.98 = 1,658 g (rounded).
She weighs 1,658 g of flakes, not 1,625 g.
She writes on her batch sheet: purity 98%, corrected caustic soda 1,658 g.
Next month she buys a different brand labelled 99% and recalculates: 1,625 / 0.99 = 1,641 g.
Amina's bars receive the sodium hydroxide the recipe intends, even when the brand changes. A 33 g difference on one run is enough to change how mild or oily a bar feels.
Water

Use **clean, soft water**: distilled water, rain water collected in a clean container and filtered, or boiled and cooled tap or borehole water. Hard or iron-rich water can cause spots and scum in the bar. Sachet or bottled water is acceptable for small test batches.

A small business may mix more than 1.5 kg of caustic soda in one go. The solution gets very hot and gives off fumes. In hot process you also cook soap paste over a flame for an hour or more. The risks are the same as at home, but larger. This lesson turns safety into a fixed routine.
Protective safety goggles
Sealed goggles stay on from the moment the caustic soda bag opens until the soap is in the mould.
Protective equipment
**Sealed chemical splash goggles**, not ordinary glasses. A face shield on top is wise when mixing large lye solutions.
**Long nitrile or rubber gloves** covering the wrists. Replace them when torn.
**Long sleeves, apron, trousers or long wrapper, closed shoes.** Synthetic fabrics melt near flames; cotton is safer around the burner.
**Dust mask** while weighing flakes or pouring washing soda powder.

Materials move in one direction so caustic soda never crosses paths with food, children or customers.
Mix lye outdoors or under a roof with open sides, upwind of yourself. Never in a closed kitchen.
Keep a clear path between lye station and cooking area so you are not carrying hot solution past people.
Put the gas cylinder outside the room or at least 1 metre from the burner, and check hoses for cracks.
Keep children, pets and visitors out of the area during production. Put a sign on the door.
Keep a fire extinguisher or a bucket of sand near the burner. Never pour water on burning oil.
Mixing lye at production scale
Put on goggles, gloves and sleeves before opening the bag.
Weigh the water into a strong stainless steel or heavy HDPE plastic container (recycling numbers 2 or 5). Use cold water; in hot weather some makers use part ice.
Weigh the caustic soda in a separate dry container.
**Add the caustic soda to the water, slowly, stirring with a stainless spoon. Never pour water onto caustic soda.**
Step back from the fumes for a minute. The solution can heat above 80 degrees Celsius.
Cover loosely, label it, and let it cool where it cannot be knocked over.

Never use aluminium, tin or zinc pots or spoons. The US National Institute for Occupational Safety and Health (NIOSH) lists these metals as reacting dangerously with sodium hydroxide; aluminium releases flammable hydrogen gas.
First aid for caustic soda

**Skin:** remove soaked clothing and flush with plenty of running water straight away, for at least 15 minutes. Do not use vinegar; water is the correct treatment. **Eyes:** rinse immediately with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to hospital. **Swallowed:** rinse the mouth, do not make the person vomit, and get medical help immediately. **Fumes:** move to fresh air. Keep a large container of clean water or a running tap within reach every time you work.
Hot process adds heat risks
Use a heavy-bottomed stainless steel pot no more than about two-thirds full. Soap paste can swell and foam over.
Keep the flame low. Stir with a long stainless paddle so your arms stay away from the pot.
Hot soap paste sticks to skin and burns like hot porridge. Treat burns with cool running water for 20 minutes and seek care for large burns.
Never leave a pot on the flame unattended.
Cleaning up after a run
Keep goggles and gloves on while cleaning. Soap paste on pots and paddles is still caustic until it has fully reacted.
Scrape leftover paste into a mould or tray rather than washing it down the drain, and let it harden.
Wash tools in hot water with gloves on; many makers let used tools sit for a day so leftover paste turns into soap and washes off easily.
Rinse empty caustic soda bags or tubs, close them and keep them away from children before disposal. Never reuse them for food or water.
Wipe tables and floors with a damp cloth to pick up stray flakes, which can burn bare feet.

Professional soap makers write formulas as **percentages of the total oil weight**, not as cups or tins. Percentages let you make a 1 kg test batch today and a 10 kg production run next week from the same formula, with no guessing.
A person working with a large calculator
Every batch starts on paper or in a calculator, never by eye.
The four numbers in every formula
**Oil percentages:** for example 70% PKO and 30% palm oil. They must add up to 100%.
**SAP value** for each oil: grams of sodium hydroxide that 1 g of that oil needs to become soap.
**Superfat:** the percentage you reduce the caustic soda by, so some oil stays free.
**Lye concentration:** caustic soda as a percentage of the caustic soda plus water. 33% is a common, workable figure.

Worked example: a 1 kg laundry test batch at two superfats
For example, Blessing in Aba wants to test a laundry formula of 70% PKO and 30% palm oil before making a big run. She makes a 1,000 g test batch.
Grams of oil: PKO 70% of 1,000 g = 700 g; palm oil 30% = 300 g.
Caustic soda at 0% superfat: 700 x 0.176 = 123.2 g; 300 x 0.142 = 42.6 g; total 165.8 g.
At 2% superfat (laundry): 165.8 x 0.98 = 162.5 g.
For comparison, at 5% superfat (bath): 165.8 x 0.95 = 157.5 g. The difference is only 5 g per kilogram of oil.
Water at 33% lye concentration: 162.5 x 67 / 33 = 330 g (rounded).
Her caustic soda is 98% pure, so she weighs 162.5 / 0.98 = 165.8 g, rounded to 166 g of flakes.

Blessing's test batch sheet reads: PKO 700 g, palm oil 300 g, caustic soda flakes 166 g (98%), water 330 g, superfat 2%. Because 5 g changes the superfat by 3 points, she uses a scale that reads in 1 g steps.
Why the water formula works

Lye concentration is caustic soda divided by (caustic soda + water). If the caustic soda is 33 parts, the water must be 67 parts. So water = caustic soda x 67 / 33. Less water (higher concentration) gives a harder bar sooner but traces faster. More water gives more working time. For hot process, many makers use a little extra water so the paste stays workable during the cook.
Weighing and rounding rules
Weigh every ingredient, including water, in grams. Never measure caustic soda or oils by cups, tins or spoons.
Round caustic soda to the nearest whole gram only at the final step. Keep one decimal place in the working.
Tare (zero) the scale with the empty container on it before each weighing.
Write each weight on the batch sheet as you weigh it, and tick it. If you are interrupted, you will know where you stopped.
For a production run, ask a second person to read back the caustic soda weight before it goes into the water.

Choose the superfat by product. In this course we use **2% for laundry bars** (within the 3% maximum recommended for laundry soap) and **5% for bath bars**. A very small superfat in a laundry bar is a safety margin: oils vary slightly and scales are not perfect, so a 0% formula can end up with a little free caustic soda.
Scaling up

To scale, multiply every gram figure by the same factor, or go back to percentages. A 10 kg run of Blessing's formula is simply ten times the 1 kg sheet: 7,000 g PKO, 3,000 g palm oil, and the caustic soda and water recalculated in the same way. Recalculate rather than multiply rounded numbers, so small rounding errors do not grow.
Never swap the alkali
SAP values for sodium hydroxide and potassium hydroxide are different. A recipe calculated for one must never be made with the other. If an online recipe does not say which it uses, do not use it.
Check in SoapCalc

In SoapCalc, choose NaOH, enter your oil weights, set the superfat and lye concentration, and press Calculate. Compare its caustic soda figure with yours. A difference of 1 or 2 g per kilogram comes from slightly different SAP values; a large difference means a mistake.

In **cold process**, the soap is poured into the mould soon after it thickens and finishes reacting on its own over a day or two, then cures for weeks. In **hot process**, you keep heating the soap paste in the pot until the reaction is complete before it goes into the mould. For laundry bars, hot process suits a small business: the soap is fully reacted on the day, mistakes show up in the pot rather than weeks later, and bars only need a short drying period to harden.
A pan cooking on a stove
Hot process means cooking the soap paste gently until the reaction is complete.
Equipment for a 10 kg-oil run
Heavy-bottomed **stainless steel pot of at least 30 litres**. The batch weighs about 15 kg and swells while cooking.
Gas burner with a steady low flame, or a heat diffuser plate.
**Platform scale** for kilograms and a kitchen scale reading in 1 g steps for the caustic soda.
A long **stainless paddle**, and either a heavy-duty stick blender or a drill mixer with a stainless paddle. Hand stirring alone at this size can take a very long time to reach trace.
Thermometer, pH test strips, wooden or plastic block moulds lined with plastic sheet, a cutting wire or long knife, and drying racks.
All the protective equipment from Module 1.
Worked example: the batch sheet for a 10 kg-oil run
For example, Chinyere in Owerri makes laundry bars from 70% PKO and 30% palm oil at 2% superfat, with 98% caustic soda flakes and 33% lye concentration.
Oils: PKO 7,000 g, palm oil 3,000 g; total 10,000 g.
Caustic soda at 0% superfat: 7,000 x 0.176 = 1,232 g; 3,000 x 0.142 = 426 g; total 1,658 g.
At 2% superfat: 1,658 x 0.98 = 1,625 g pure sodium hydroxide (rounded).
Corrected for 98% purity: 1,625 / 0.98 = 1,658 g of flakes to weigh.
Total wet batch: 10,000 + 1,658 + 3,299 = 14,957 g, about 15 kg.
Chinyere expects about 15 kg of fresh soap. After trimming about 300 g of edges, she can cut 73 bars of 200 g each. She checks the figures in SoapCalc before production day.
The production run, step by step
**Prepare.** Clear the area, put on protective equipment, and lay out every weighed material with its label. Tick each one on the batch sheet.
**Make the lye solution** outdoors: add 1,658 g of flakes slowly to 3,299 g of cold water in a stainless or HDPE container. Let it cool for about an hour.
**Melt the oils** in the big pot on low heat. PKO and palm oil are often semi-solid in cool weather. Turn off the heat once they are fully liquid.

**Combine.** Pour the lye solution slowly into the oils, down the paddle, with the flame off. Blend in short bursts and stir in between until the mixture thickens to **trace**: a drizzle leaves a trail on the surface.

**Cook.** Cover and heat on the lowest flame. Stir every 10 to 15 minutes. The paste thickens, may rise and foam (stir it down, do not let it overflow), then becomes smoother and partly translucent, a bit like petroleum jelly. A large batch often takes one to two hours; it is ready by test, not by the clock.
**Test** a small cooled sample (see below). If it fails, keep cooking and test again after 15 minutes.
**Mould.** Turn off the gas. Scoop the hot paste into lined moulds and press and bang the moulds firmly to push out air pockets. Smooth the top.

**Cut and dry.** The next day, unmould and cut bars with a wire or knife. Stamp your mark if you use one. Stand bars on racks with space between them, in a shaded, airy room, for one to two weeks before packing.

Is the cook finished?

Take a pea-sized lump, let it cool, rub it with a little water and test the lather with a **pH strip**. Well-made soap commonly reads about 9 to 10. A reading of 11 or more, or a lump that still looks oily or wet in the middle, means unreacted caustic soda or oil remains: keep cooking. Phenolphthalein drops turn pink in all soap, so they cannot tell finished soap from lye-heavy soap on their own.
Hot paste and fresh soap

Hot soap paste is as dangerous as hot oil and still caustic until the cook is complete. Wear gloves and goggles throughout, keep a long paddle, and keep children away from moulds. Treat any splash with running water straight away.
Why laundry bars still need drying
Hot process completes the reaction, but the bars still hold water. One to two weeks on racks makes them harder, so they last longer in a wet bucket and customers get more washes from each bar.
Hot process finishes the reaction in the pot, so batch faults show on the day

Many customers like powder for buckets and machines. Big factories make synthetic detergent powders by spray drying, which is beyond a small workshop. What you can make well is a **soap-based laundry powder**: your own dried laundry soap, grated fine, blended with **washing soda** (sodium carbonate, also called soda ash). It is also a good way to use offcuts and misshapen bars.
A bucket
A soap and washing soda powder is designed for bucket washing and top-loading machines.
What washing soda does

Washing soda is an alkaline salt. It softens hard water by tying up calcium and magnesium so they do not waste your soap as scum. It also helps lift greasy and sweat stains. It is not caustic soda and does not make soap by itself, but it is still an irritant: its dust stings eyes and the powder can dry and redden skin.
Handling washing soda

Wear gloves, goggles and a dust mask when pouring and blending. Blend with a lid on or in a closed container. Label the finished powder clearly, keep it away from children and food, and do not sell it in food or drink containers.
Making the powder
Use only fully dried hot-process laundry bars (at least one week on the rack). Wet soap clumps.
Grate the bars finely with a stainless grater or a dedicated grinder kept only for soap.
Spread the gratings on a clean tray in a shaded, airy room for a few days until they snap rather than bend.
Weigh grated soap and washing soda for your chosen ratio, for example 1 part soap to 1 part washing soda by weight for a first trial.
Blend in a closed container: shake or tumble until evenly mixed. Optional: a small amount of fragrance stirred in at the end.
Pack into sealed, labelled pouches or tubs at once, because powder absorbs moisture and cakes.

Bath Soap Production

Bath bars are judged by how they feel on skin, so this module is about balance: a quick melt-and-pour line for gifts and samples, a cold-process bath bar designed with SoapCalc's quality numbers at a 5% superfat, and safe, honest use of additives, colours and scents.
Melt-and-pour bath bars for gifts, samples and quick orders
Explain what melt-and-pour base is and when it makes business sense
Melt, scent and pour a base without overheating it
Prevent bubbles and glycerin sweat in humid weather
Cost a melt-and-pour bar from your own receipts

**Melt-and-pour** soap uses a ready-made soap base that a factory has already saponified. You melt it, add scent and colour, and pour it into moulds. There is no caustic soda to handle and bars can be used as soon as they set. The trade-off is cost: you pay for someone else's soap, so each bar costs more and you control fewer ingredients. Many small makers use melt-and-pour for event gifts, hotel samples, children's shapes and fast orders, and cold process for their main bath line.
A person holding a gift box
Melt-and-pour is ideal for gift sets, souvenirs and quick custom orders.
Choosing a base
**Clear glycerin base:** transparent, good for embedding shapes and bright colours.
**White base:** opaque, pastel colours.
**Speciality bases** such as goat milk or shea: sold by suppliers with their own ingredient list.
Ask the supplier for the full ingredient list (INCI names) and the recommended melting and pouring temperature. You will need the ingredient list for your label.
Making a batch
Cut the base into small, even cubes so it melts evenly.

Melt gently in a double boiler (a bowl over a pot of hot water) or in a microwave in short bursts, stirring between bursts. **Never let it boil.** Overheated base turns thick, rubbery and yellowish and may smell burnt.
Take it off the heat. Stir in colour, then fragrance at the rate on the supplier's sheet. Stir slowly to avoid bubbles.
Pour into clean, dry moulds at the temperature the supplier recommends.
Spray the surface lightly with **isopropyl alcohol (rubbing alcohol, 99%)** to pop bubbles.
Leave to set for a few hours, unmould, and **wrap each bar in cling film or shrink film straight away**.
Melt-and-pour in five moves
Cube the base
Melt gently, never boil
Add colour and scent
Pour and spray alcohol
Unmould and wrap
Wrapping straight after unmoulding stops glycerin sweat in humid air.
Layers and embeds
Pour the first layer and let it form a skin that holds when pressed lightly.
Spray the surface with alcohol, which helps the next layer stick.
Pour the second layer slightly cooler than the first, so it does not melt through.
For embeds, cut small cubes of a contrasting colour from an earlier bar, spray them with alcohol and place them in the mould before pouring clear base over them.

Because the base is already soap, the price per kilogram is higher than for oils and caustic soda. Melt-and-pour makes most sense for small, custom or gift orders where design and speed matter more than the lowest cost per bar. For your everyday bath line, a cold-process formula you calculate yourself is usually cheaper per bar and fully under your control.

Your label must list the base's full ingredient list as given by the supplier, followed by what you added, such as fragrance (Parfum) and colour. Keep the supplier's sheet with your batch records so you can show where each ingredient came from.
Glycerin sweat

Melt-and-pour bases contain extra glycerin, which pulls water from the air. In humid places such as Lagos, Port Harcourt or Calabar, unwrapped bars soon look wet and beaded, which customers often mistake for a fault. Wrap bars tightly as soon as they are unmoulded and store them in a closed container.
Alcohol and heat

Isopropyl alcohol is highly flammable. Never spray it near a gas flame or a hot stove ring, and keep the bottle closed and away from children. Melted base can burn skin: pour slowly and keep a bowl of cool water nearby for burns.

Mix the lye solution outdoors with full protective equipment and let it cool.
Melt the palm oil, PKO and shea, then add the olive and castor oil, which cools the mix.

Fragrance and essential oils
Use only cosmetic-grade fragrance oils or essential oils from a supplier who gives a safety data sheet and a maximum use rate for soap. **Never exceed that rate.**

Never add mercury or bleaching agents

The World Health Organization warns that skin-lightening products containing mercury are dangerous, and the Minamata Convention on Mercury restricts the manufacture, import and export of mercury-added cosmetics. Do not add mercury compounds, skin-bleaching chemicals, antibiotics or steroid creams to soap, and do not sell soap as a skin lightener.
Colour from local ingredients

You can colour bath bars without synthetic dyes. Red palm oil in the formula gives warm orange tones. Kaolin gives a soft cream. Activated charcoal gives grey to black. Turmeric gives yellow but may mark towels. Natural colours can fade in sunlight, so store bars away from windows and tell customers that colour may soften over time.

Fragrance is calculated from the weight of oils, not the whole batch. For 1,000 g of oils at 2%, use 20 g; at 3%, 30 g. If the supplier's maximum is lower than the rate you planned, use the supplier's figure. Weigh fragrance on the 1 g scale and add it at light trace, stirring well.
Cosmetic claims, not medical claims

A soap cleans. You may say it "cleans gently", "has a light citrus scent" or "contains shea butter". You may not say it "cures eczema", "treats acne", "kills all germs" or "removes dark spots". Medical claims make your product a drug in the eyes of regulators such as NAFDAC, and they mislead customers. If a customer has a skin condition, advise them to see a health worker.

Worked example: from total cost to prices
For example, Chinyere's run gives 73 bars with a net weight of 180 g. She sells most bars wholesale to traders and some retail from her shop.
Cost per bar: 42,540 / 73 = 583 naira (rounded).
Wholesale price: she sets 750 naira per bar. Profit per bar: 750 minus 583 = 167 naira.
Retail price: 900 naira per bar. Profit per bar: 900 minus 583 = 317 naira.
She expects to sell 48 bars wholesale and 25 retail: 48 x 750 = 36,000 naira; 25 x 900 = 22,500 naira; total sales 58,500 naira.
Profit for the run: 58,500 minus 42,540 = 15,960 naira, after paying her helpers and overheads.
Chinyere knows her floor price is 583 naira per bar. Any discount below that loses money, and every run that sells as planned earns about 16,000 naira on top of wages.

Price starts from your own cost, then is checked against the market, never the other way round.
Markup and margin are different

**Markup** is profit divided by cost. **Margin** is profit divided by price. At 750 naira wholesale, Chinyere's profit of 167 naira is a markup of 167 / 583 = 29% but a margin of 167 / 750 = 22%. At 900 naira retail, the markup is 54% and the margin 35%. Know which one a buyer or lender is asking about, because the numbers are different.

Use the same cost sheet for your other products. For laundry powder, the cost of the soap is your own cost per kilogram of bars, not the retail price. For bath bars, add fragrance, additives and the extra weeks of curing space, and remember a cold-process bath batch ties up money for 4 to 6 weeks before it can be sold.
When prices rise

Rerun the cost sheet whenever a main material changes price. If PKO rises from 2,600 to 3,000 naira per kg, Chinyere's 7 kg costs 2,800 naira more. Her run now costs 42,540 + 2,800 = 45,340 naira, and her cost per bar rises from 583 to 621 naira. Her wholesale profit per bar falls from 167 to 129 naira. She can absorb this for a short time, but if the higher price holds, she must adjust her prices or her formula, and tell her regular buyers early.
Recovering equipment costs

Equipment is bought once and used for many runs. Suppose Chinyere's 30 litre pot, mixer, moulds, scales and racks cost 150,000 naira (example figure). With a profit of 15,960 naira per run, she needs 150,000 / 15,960 = 9.4, so about **10 runs** to pay back the equipment. At one run a week, that is about ten weeks.
What changes the cost per bar
**Waste:** a failed batch still costs the full 42,540 naira. Quality control protects your profit.
**Bar size:** cutting 200 g wet bars instead of 220 g gives more bars per run, but the label must still be honest.
**Buying in bulk:** a 25 kg bag of caustic soda or a drum of PKO usually costs less per kilogram, but only if you can store it safely and use it before it spoils.
**Fragrance:** laundry bars sell well unscented; adding fragrance raises cost per bar.
Pay yourself

Include your own time as labour, even if you work alone. If the business only makes money when your time is free, it is not yet a business. Raise prices, cut waste or scale the run before you agree to sell below cost.

Why this matters
Production means bigger risks
Know why laundry and bath bars differ

Soap is made by reacting oils with caustic soda, which is sodium hydroxide. This reaction, saponification, gives soap and glycerin.
At home you buy one bottle of oil. In production you buy kegs, drums and bags, so a bad purchase hurts more.
You may mix more than 1.5 kg of caustic soda at once, so the risks are larger.
And every bar depends on weighing the right grams.
Two design goals
Laundry bar or bath bar?
A laundry bar works on fabric. It must cut grease, stay hard in a wet bucket, and leave no oil on clothes. So it uses mostly palm kernel oil, called PKO, or coconut oil.
A bath bar touches skin every day, so it balances cleansing oils with conditioning oils.
The spare oil left in the bar is called the superfat. In this course we use 2% for laundry bars and 5% for bath bars.
Before you buy
Check every raw material
PKO: clear to light yellow, clean nutty smell
Never use oil that was used for frying
Caustic soda: sealed, dry flakes, purity printed
Log supplier, date and purity
PKO is the backbone of Nigerian laundry bars. It should be clear to light yellow when warm and smell clean and nutty. A sour smell means it is going rancid.
Never use frying oil. Food bits make soap smell bad and spoil faster.
Buy caustic soda in sealed bags. Clumped flakes have lost strength. Look for the purity on the bag, for example 98%.
Use distilled water, filtered rain water, or boiled and cooled water. Hard or iron-rich water can cause spots and scum.
Write the supplier, date and purity on every container, so you can trace any bad batch.
Step by step
Caustic soda INTO water. Never water onto caustic soda.
Goggles, long gloves, sleeves on first
Weigh cold water into steel or HDPE plastic
Weigh caustic soda in a separate dry container
Add caustic soda to water slowly, stirring
Step back: it can pass 80 degrees Celsius
Cover, label, cool where it cannot fall
Mix lye outdoors or under a roof with open sides. Put on sealed goggles, long gloves and sleeves before you open the bag.
Weigh cold water into a strong stainless steel or heavy plastic container, marked 2 or 5. Never aluminium, tin or zinc.
Weigh the caustic soda in a separate, dry container.
Now add the caustic soda to the water, slowly, stirring. Never pour water onto caustic soda.
Cover it loosely, label it, and let it cool where it cannot be knocked over.

Remove soaked clothing. Flush with running water for at least 15 minutes. No vinegar.
Rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, eyelids open. Then go to hospital.
Rinse the mouth. Do not make the person vomit. Get medical help immediately.
If lye touches skin, remove soaked clothing and flush with plenty of running water for at least 15 minutes. Do not use vinegar. Water is the correct treatment.
For the eyes, rinse with clean running water for at least 15 minutes, holding the eyelids open, then go to hospital.
If it is swallowed, rinse the mouth, do not make the person vomit, and get medical help immediately. Never keep caustic soda in a drink bottle.

For example, Blessing in Aba tests a laundry formula of 70% PKO and 30% palm oil, with 1,000 g of oils.
First, percentages to grams. 700 g of PKO and 300 g of palm oil.
Next, multiply each oil by its SAP value, the grams of caustic soda one gram of that oil needs. PKO is 0.176 and palm oil is 0.142. Together that is 165.8 g.
Then subtract the superfat. At 2%, she multiplies by 0.98 and gets 162.5 g.
For water at 33% lye concentration, she multiplies by 67 and divides by 33. That is 330 g.
Her flakes are 98% pure, so she divides by 0.98 and weighs 166 g.
Only 5 g changes the superfat by 3 points, so she uses a scale that reads in 1 g steps, and checks in SoapCalc.

Production day
The 10 kg-oil run, step by step
Ready by test, not by the clock.
Prepare: protection on, tick every weighed item
Lye outdoors: 1,658 g flakes into 3,299 g water
Melt the oils on low heat, then turn it off
Combine with the flame off and blend to trace
Cook on the lowest flame, stir every 10 to 15 min
Test, then mould, cut next day and dry
For example, Chinyere in Owerri makes laundry bars from 7,000 g of PKO and 3,000 g of palm oil. Her stainless pot holds at least 30 litres, because the batch weighs about 15 kg and swells.
First, protection on, and tick every weighed material.
Outdoors, she adds 1,658 g of caustic soda flakes slowly into 3,299 g of cold water, never water onto caustic soda. It cools for about an hour.
She melts the oils in the big pot on low heat, and turns the heat off once they are liquid.
With the flame off, she pours the lye slowly down the paddle and blends in short bursts until trace, when a drizzle leaves a trail on the surface.
Then she cooks on the lowest flame, stirring every 10 to 15 minutes. If the paste foams up, she stirs it down. It turns smooth and partly see-through, like petroleum jelly.
A large batch often takes one to two hours, but it is ready by test, not by the clock. Then she moulds it, cuts bars next day, and dries them for one to two weeks.

Take a pea-sized lump, let it cool, rub it with a little water and test the lather with a pH strip. Well-made soap commonly reads about 9 to 10.
A reading of 11 or more, or a lump that is oily or wet inside, means caustic soda or oil is left. Keep cooking and test again after 15 minutes.
Keep gloves and goggles on throughout.

Turning bars into laundry powder
Use only fully dried bars
Grate fine, air-dry until gratings snap
Blend 1 part soap to 1 part washing soda

Pack at once in sealed, labelled pouches
Many customers like powder, and you can make it from your own dried bars and offcuts. Wet soap clumps, so the bars must be fully dry.
Grate them fine and spread the gratings in a shaded, airy room until they snap rather than bend.
Blend with washing soda, which softens hard water and helps lift grease. A first trial is 1 part soap to 1 part washing soda by weight.
Washing soda is not caustic soda, but its dust stings eyes and dries skin. Wear gloves, goggles and a dust mask, and blend in a closed container.
Pack it straight away, because powder takes in moisture and cakes.

Common faults
When a batch goes wrong
Too much caustic soda. Do not sell. Label it NOT FOR SALE and recheck your sums and purity.
Cook not finished, poor mixing or a weighing error. Do not sell; recheck the batch sheet.
Too much water, too little caustic soda, or too much soft oil. Dry longer; adjust next batch.
The worst fault is a pH of 11 or more, or a bar that stings. That is too much caustic soda, and it burns hands. Never sell it. If you cannot correct it with confidence, dispose of it safely.
Oily pockets mean the cook was not finished, or there was poor mixing or a weighing error. That batch is not sold either.
A soft bar usually means too much water or soft oil. Dry it longer and adjust the next batch.
Key points
Remember
Hot process shows faults on the day
Cook low, stir often, judge by test
pH 9 to 10 is normal; 11 or more, keep cooking
Powder: dried grated soap plus washing soda
Never sell lye-heavy or oily batches
To remember. Hot process finishes the reaction in the pot, so cook low and judge by test.
Make powder only from dried soap, and never sell a lye-heavy or oily batch.

Step by step
Making the cold-process batch
Fresh soap is still caustic: wear gloves to cut it.
Mix lye outdoors, full protection, let it cool
Melt hard oils, then add olive and castor
Combine warm, not hot, below about 45 C
Blend to light trace; add fragrance now
Mould, cover, wrap in a towel 24 hours
Cut after one to two days; cure 4 to 6 weeks
Mix the lye solution outdoors with full protective equipment, and let it cool.
Melt the palm oil, PKO and shea, then add the olive and castor oil.
When both are warm, not hot, pour the lye into the oils. Many makers combine below about 45 degrees Celsius.
Blend in short bursts until light trace, and add fragrance.
Pour into a lined mould, cover it and wrap it in an old towel for 24 hours.
Unmould and cut after one to two days, wearing gloves. Then cure the bars for 4 to 6 weeks in a shaded, airy room, and do a pH test before sale.
Additives
Safe starting amounts per 500 g oils
About 1 teaspoon. Mix with a little batch water first, to avoid lumps.
About 1 teaspoon. It adds heat, so keep the mould cool to avoid cracks.
Weigh from the oils, for example 2%. Never exceed the supplier's maximum rate.
Additives make a bar special, but start small and test. Kaolin clay starts at about 1 teaspoon per 500 g of oils.
Honey also starts at about 1 teaspoon. It adds heat, so do not wrap that mould in a towel.
Fragrance is weighed from the oils. At 2%, 1,000 g of oils needs 20 g. Never go above the supplier's maximum, and leave out cinnamon and clove, which can irritate skin.
Honest labels
You may say
Cleans gently
Has a light citrus scent
Contains shea butter
Never say or add
Cures eczema, treats acne
Mercury or bleaching agents
A soap cleans. You may say it cleans gently, has a light scent, or contains shea butter.
You may not say it cures eczema, treats acne or removes dark spots. Medical claims make your soap a drug in the eyes of regulators such as NAFDAC.
Never add mercury, skin-bleaching chemicals or medicines, and never sell soap as a skin lightener.
